alternativas.feedback: CORRECT. This cell is a mucus-secreting goblet cell, which is located in the lining epithelium of the small intestine. Mucus is a glycoprotein which can stain with either hematoxylin (as shown here) or eosin, depending on the composition of the mucus. Mucigen in these cells often appears vacuolated.

alternativas.feedback: CORRECT. This acinus is composed of pyramidal-shaped cells with numerous distinct secretory granules. Their contents are released by the merocrine mode of secretion. During the process of secretion, the membrane of the granule fuses with the apical plasma membrane of the cell (exocytosis) and the granule contents only are released into the lumen of the acinus.

alternativas.feedback: CORRECT. This sebaceous gland is composed of acini that branch from the hair follicle that serves as the duct. The cells of the acinus produce a thick, oily secretion that accumulates in the cells. Secretion is by the holocrine mode as entire cells are shed with their secretory contents onto the hair shaft.

alternativas.feedback: CORRECT. This low magnification image shows a compound tubulo-acinar gland in which nearly all the secretory units are mucus-secreting tubules. The more darkly stained area in the upper left contains serous-secreting acini. Also visible are numerous ducts indicating a highly branching duct system; therefore, this is a compound gland.

alternativas.feedback: CORRECT. The acinus is a spherical structure composed of pyramidal-shaped cells and forms the basic secretory unit of some glands. In this case, this acinus produces a serous product, as evidenced by the presence of distinct secretory granules, and the individual cells release their secretory product by the merocrine mode of section. Two pale-staining interlobular ducts are also visible.

alternativas.feedback: CORRECT. This is an example of a sheet gland which consists of an epithelium composed entirely of mucus-secreting goblet cells. The best example of a sheet gland is that which lines the stomach, seen here. The mucous secretions of these cells protect the stomach lining from the acidic contents.
